1.title: AI Risk Management & Impact Assessments
1.text: In the last module we built the program. Now we run its engine. This module is AI risk management — the repeatable process you apply to every system in your inventory — and the impact assessments that document it.

1.title: Risk Management Is the Engine
1.text: Think back to the program we built — the roles, the committee, the inventory. All of that is the vehicle. Risk management is the engine that makes it move. It's the thing you actually do to each AI system: the concrete process of finding what could go wrong, working out how bad it is, and reducing it. Everything else — the policies, the org chart, the frameworks — exists to support this loop. So if someone asks you what AI governance actually does, day to day, this is the honest answer: it runs a risk process on every AI system, over and over.

1.title: The AI Risk Lifecycle
1.text: The process is a five-stage loop. Identify the risks. Assess them. Prioritize them. Treat them. And monitor — which loops you right back to identifying new risks. If you've done any risk management before — in security, in finance, in safety — this will look familiar, because it is classic risk management. But it's tuned for AI's specific characteristics: the central role of data, the opacity of models, the autonomy of agentic systems, and the way models drift over time. And that last point is why this is a loop, not a project. You don't risk-assess an AI system once and file it away. You keep turning the loop for the system's entire life.

1.title: Identify — Where AI Risk Comes From
1.text: Stage one: identify. The goal is to surface what could go wrong — and the trap is only finding the risks you already expected. So you work from a structured taxonomy, like the harm families from Module 2, and you pull from every source: the data, the model itself, the context it's used in, the people it affects, and any third-party components you've built on. And you ask three disciplined questions for each: what could go wrong, for whom, and at which stage of the lifecycle? The structure matters because human intuition is biased toward familiar risks. A taxonomy forces you to consider the privacy risk, the security risk, the societal risk — not just the one that's top of mind today.

1.title: Assess — Likelihood × Impact, AI-Tuned
1.text: Stage two: assess. The classic move is to rate each risk on two axes — how likely is it, and how bad would it be — and plot it on a matrix from green to red. That still applies. But for AI you weight some specific factors. The scale of deployment: is this touching ten people or ten million? The autonomy level: does a human review each decision, or does the system act alone? Reversibility: can you undo the harm? Who's affected, and how vulnerable are they? How explainable is it? And how severe is the worst-case harm? The one I'd underline is scale. Scale is what turns an ordinary AI bug into a mass harm — one flawed model can wrong thousands of people simultaneously, which a human decision-maker never could.

1.title: Prioritize — Against Appetite & Tiers
1.text: Stage three: prioritize — because you can't fix everything at once, and pretending you can just paralyzes the program. So you triage. You run every risk through your organization's stated risk appetite and your thresholds, and you sort them into buckets: accept it, watch it, or treat it now. And you tie this to the risk tiers we've discussed — a high-risk system gets the deepest, most rigorous treatment, while a minimal-risk system gets a light touch. Governance is fundamentally triage. The skill isn't treating every risk equally; it's concentrating your limited effort where the stakes are genuinely high.

1.title: Treat — The Four Options
1.text: Stage four: treat. You have exactly four options for any risk — the four T's. Tolerate: accept it, if it's within your risk appetite, and document that decision. Treat: actively mitigate it — and this is where most of the work happens, through bias mitigation, human oversight, guardrails, better data, which we'll detail next module. Transfer: shift the risk through a contract, insurance, or vendor obligations. Or terminate: decide not to build or deploy the system at all. Most AI risk gets treated — actively reduced with controls. But a mature program always keeps "terminate" on the table. The willingness to say "no, we shouldn't build this" is what separates real governance from a rubber stamp.

1.title: Monitor — Because AI Drifts
1.text: Stage five: monitor — and for AI this is non-negotiable, for one reason that doesn't apply to most other systems. AI drifts. A model that was fair and accurate on launch day can become unfair and inaccurate over time, as the real world diverges from its training data. So you continuously track its performance, its bias metrics over time, signs of data drift, incident reports, and changes in how it's being used. When that performance line starts sliding — model decay — an alert fires and you go back to the top of the loop. A model you deployed and forgot is a model that is, slowly and invisibly, going wrong.

1.title: Impact Assessments — AIA & FRIA
1.text: Now, the formal, documented front-end of all this: impact assessments. Two terms to know. An algorithmic or AI impact assessment — an AIA — is a structured evaluation of a system's effects on people and society. And a fundamental-rights impact assessment — a FRIA — is a specific duty the EU AI Act places on certain deployers of high-risk systems, focused on impacts to people's rights. Both walk through a similar question set: who is affected, what rights are at stake, what's the worst case, and what mitigations and recourse exist? Here's the key shift: these used to be best practice. Now, for many high-risk deployments, they're a legal requirement. So learning to run a solid impact assessment is rapidly becoming a core professional skill.

1.title: Conformity Assessment — Proving It to the Law
1.text: There's a related but distinct concept under the EU AI Act: conformity assessment. Where an impact assessment looks at effects on people, conformity assessment is about proving, before you put a high-risk system on the market, that it actually meets all the Act's requirements. The path runs: high-risk system, then a conformity assessment — sometimes a self-assessment, sometimes requiring a third party depending on the system type — then technical documentation and a declaration of conformity, then CE marking, then registration in the EU database. It's the same logic the EU already uses for physical product safety, now applied to AI. It's how the law makes you demonstrate compliance up front, rather than just promising it.

1.title: Helios Runs the Impact Assessment
1.text: Let's watch this pay off at Helios. Helios runs a fundamental-rights impact assessment on its hiring tool — and it catches something. The affected group: all applicants. The rights at stake: non-discrimination, privacy, dignity. And the finding, flagged red: the selection rate for women is just sixty-eight percent of the rate for men. That's a classic disparate-impact red flag — in fact, it's below the common four-fifths threshold used in employment law. The worst case is systematic discrimination, at scale, plus serious legal liability. So the assessment requires mitigation before go-live, human oversight, and a recourse path for candidates. And notice what just happened: the assessment did its job. It caught the bias on paper, before deployment — not after a lawsuit, not after a damaging headline. That is the entire purpose of impact assessment.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: To recap: risk management is the engine — a continuous loop of identify, assess, prioritize, treat, and monitor. Weight the AI-specific factors, especially scale. Treat risks by tolerating, treating, transferring, or terminating. Monitor relentlessly, because AI drifts. And impact assessments — the AIA and the EU's FRIA — plus conformity assessment are the documented, increasingly mandatory front-end. Helios caught its bias in the assessment, before launch. Next, in Module 9, we go inside the lifecycle to see the development and deployment controls that actually treat the risks we've found.
